title: Reading the Science of Reading
author: Terry Underwood
summary: Terry Underwood distinguishes capital-S Science from the everyday scientific work teachers do, then argues that the Science of Reading has narrowed into a trademark for an autonomous, decoding-centered model of literacy. He illustrates what the science can offer by describing his own dissertation, in which three middle school English teachers gave up grading in favor of a portfolio system judged by a teacher jury, with goal-orientation research by Dweck and Deci guiding the design. His survey data showed a modest but statistically significant gain in intrinsic motivation for the portfolio classes. He then surveys a century of internal disagreement in reading research, from drills and readability formulas to remediation, and contrasts Brian Street's autonomous and ideological models of literacy. His warning is that fidelity enforcement, commercial materials and surveillance erode teachers' professional agency, when teachers should be able to act as scientists of their own classrooms.
points: Motivation to read is treated as a learning outcome that can be taught and graded, not a given, and a portfolio assessment system moved middle schoolers measurably toward intrinsic motivation.
Extrinsic rewards such as grades, points and pizza can crowd out the intrinsic motivation that schools actually want, and school culture raises their salience every year.
The author reads current reading-science debates as a conflict between reading as a technical, autonomous skill and reading as a cultural, ideological practice.
The Science of Reading label has become entangled with commercial materials, high-stakes testing and fidelity enforcement, which erodes teachers' agency to question and test methods.
Researchers themselves worry that science is being defined too narrowly, and a recent panel urged choosing designs that fit the question rather than questions that fit numbers.
